entries.topicDescription: Working effectively with Kotlin's type system, nullability, and smart casts.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the '!!' operator in Kotlin?
questions.explanation: The '!!' operator is used to assert that a value is not null. If the value is null, it throws a NullPointerException.

answers.answerText: To assert that a value is not null and throw an exception if it is
To safely access a nullable value without throwing an exception
To convert a nullable type to a non-nullable type
To check if a value is null and return a default value

entries.topicDescription: Structured concurrency with suspend functions, builders, and dispatchers.

questions.questionText: What does the 'suspend' keyword indicate on a Kotlin function?
questions.explanation: 'suspend' marks a function that can pause and resume execution at certain points without blocking the underlying thread. It doesn't by itself decide which thread the function runs on — that's the dispatcher's job.

answers.answerText: That the function can be paused and resumed without blocking the thread
That the function runs on a background thread automatically
That the function is asynchronous like JavaScript's async/await
That the function can only be called from a coroutine builder

questions.questionText: What is the key difference between the 'launch' and 'async' coroutine builders?
questions.explanation: 'launch' is fire-and-forget and returns a Job with no result. 'async' is used when you need a return value — it returns a Deferred<T> that you call .await() on.

answers.answerText: 'launch' returns a Job with no result; 'async' returns a Deferred you can await
'launch' always runs on Dispatchers.IO; 'async' always runs on Dispatchers.Main
'launch' is for suspend functions only; 'async' is for regular functions
'async' blocks the calling thread while 'launch' never does

entries.topicDescription: Transforming and querying Kotlin's List, Set, and Map types.

questions.questionText: What is the key difference between 'map' and 'flatMap' on a Kotlin collection?
questions.explanation: 'map' transforms each element one-to-one. 'flatMap' transforms each element into its own collection, then flattens all of those collections into a single list.

answers.answerText: 'flatMap' flattens the nested collections produced by the transform into one list
'map' is lazy while 'flatMap' is always eager
'flatMap' only works on Sequences, never on Lists
'map' mutates the original collection but 'flatMap' doesn't

entries.topicDescription: Choosing between let, run, with, apply, and also.

questions.questionText: Which scope function is typically used to configure an object, returning the object itself rather than the lambda's result?
questions.explanation: 'apply' runs its lambda with the object as the receiver ('this') and returns that same object — ideal for configuration or builder-style chains. 'let' and 'run' return the lambda's result instead.

answers.answerText: apply
let
run
with

questions.questionText: Inside a 'let' block, how do you refer to the receiver by default?
questions.explanation: 'let' passes the receiver into the lambda as the argument 'it' (unless you rename it), whereas 'run', 'with', and 'apply' expose it as 'this'.

answers.answerText: it
this
self
receiver

entries.topicDescription: Modeling data and fixed-state hierarchies idiomatically.

questions.questionText: What does Kotlin automatically generate for a 'data class'?
questions.explanation: Declaring 'data class' has the compiler generate equals()/hashCode() from the primary constructor properties, a readable toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions for destructuring.

answers.answerText: equals(), hashCode(), toString(), and copy()
Only a no-argument constructor
A companion object with a builder function
Getters and setters, but not equals() or hashCode()

questions.questionText: Why use a 'sealed class' instead of a plain open class to represent a fixed set of states?
questions.explanation: All direct subclasses of a sealed class must be known at compile time (same module/package), so the compiler can verify a 'when' over it is exhaustive — catching missing cases as compile errors instead of runtime bugs.

answers.answerText: The compiler can exhaustively check 'when' expressions over it without needing an 'else' branch
Sealed classes are faster at runtime than open classes
Sealed classes can be freely subclassed from any module
Sealed classes automatically implement Parcelable

entries.topicDescription: Adding behavior to existing types without inheritance.

questions.questionText: Are Kotlin extension functions resolved statically or dynamically?
questions.explanation: Extension functions are resolved statically — which one gets called is decided by the declared (compile-time) type of the expression, not its actual runtime type. That's also why they can't truly override member functions.

answers.answerText: Statically, based on the declared type of the expression at compile time
Dynamically, based on the runtime type, just like member functions
Statically for classes but dynamically for interfaces
It depends on whether the extension is declared 'open'

entries.topicDescription: Variance, bounds, and type-safe generic APIs.

questions.questionText: What does the 'out' variance modifier mean on a Kotlin generic type parameter?
questions.explanation: 'out T' declares T covariant: the class can only produce/return T (e.g. in return positions), which is what lets a List<Cat> be used where a List<Animal> is expected. 'in T' is the contravariant counterpart, restricting T to consumer/parameter positions.

answers.answerText: The type parameter is covariant — only produced (returned), never consumed as a parameter
The type parameter is contravariant — only consumed, never produced
The type parameter must be an open class
The type parameter is erased at runtime, unlike other generics
